title: Costs & revenues
examples: What is the difference between short run and long run costs?
How does increasing size affect a business's costs?
Can a business ever have diseconomies of scale?

explain.say: Today we explore how costs and revenues change. We will look at different time periods for businesses.
In the short run, some costs are fixed. These costs do not change with output levels.

draw.text: Fixed Costs: Don't change with output

explain.say: In the long run, all costs are variable. A business can change all its inputs as needed.

draw.text: Long Run: All costs are variable

explain.say: Economies of scale describe cost changes with size. Bigger firms can sometimes lower their average costs.

draw.text: Economies of Scale: Lower average costs

explain.say: Diseconomies of scale happen when a firm gets too big. Management issues can raise average costs again.
Imagine a local bakery needing a large oven. This is a real-life fixed cost in the short run.

faq.q: What is the main difference between short run and long run?
faq.a: The main difference is that in the short run, at least one input cannot be changed. In the long run, all inputs are considered variable.
asks: When can a business change all its inputs?
Does the time frame matter for costs?

faq.a: Economies of scale happen because larger firms can spread overhead costs over more units. This lowers the average cost per unit.
asks: Why do big companies save money?
What makes a firm more efficient as it grows?

faq.a: Diseconomies of scale occur when a firm becomes too large, leading to coordination problems. These problems increase the average cost per unit.
asks: Can growing too much hurt a business?
What is the limit to company size?

faq.q: Is there an ideal size for a company?
faq.a: Yes, there is often an optimal scale where average costs are at their minimum. This is the point before diseconomies set in.
asks: Where is the best size for a business?
What is the minimum cost size?

faq.a: Fixed costs are expenses that do not change regardless of how much the business produces in the short run. Think of rent payments.
asks: What costs are not related to output?

facts: In the short run, fixed inputs cannot be changed by the firm.
Long run analysis assumes that all factors of production are variable.
Economies of scale mean that average costs fall as output increases.
Diseconomies of scale suggest that average costs rise after a certain size.

quiz.say: A car manufacturer decides to build an entirely new factory to increase production capacity. This decision relates to:
quiz.why: Building a new factory means changing the scale of the fixed input, which is only possible in the long run.

wrong.1: In the short run, the size of the factory is fixed, so this change is impossible.
wrong.2: This is a change in capacity, not just a cost category.
wrong.3: While it might cause economies, the action described is about the time frame, not just the cost effect.

quiz.say: A small bookstore owner must pay the same monthly rent whether they sell one book or one thousand books. This rent represents:
quiz.why: Rent is a cost that does not change based on the number of books sold in the short term.

wrong.1: Variable costs change directly with the number of books sold.
wrong.2: Opportunity cost is what is given up, not a recurring payment like rent.
wrong.3: Average cost is a ratio, whereas rent is a total fixed amount.

quiz.say: A global tech company finds that coordinating its massive international operations leads to slow decision-making and increased waste. This situation best illustrates:
quiz.why: Diseconomies of scale relate to management and coordination problems when a firm becomes excessively large.

wrong.0: While costs increase, the underlying cause is structural inefficiency, not just material costs.
wrong.2: Economies of scale imply that costs are falling due to size, which is the opposite of the scenario.
wrong.3: This problem is related to the overall size and structure, not just a temporary input constraint.
